results.corrected_title: OpenAI and Anthropic tell UK MPs AI safety rules should be binding; Google DeepMind and Meta hold back
results.corrected_summary: On 13 October 2026 the House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee, chaired by Liam Byrne, heard evidence on AI safety from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta. Anthropic's Liam Booth-Smith said the rules should be binding. OpenAI's Tom Duff Gordon backed a statutory framework and an international convention, with incident reporting as a first mandatory step. Google DeepMind and Meta did not support new legislation, and officials confirmed that the UK regime is voluntary and that the AI Security Institute (AISI) cannot stop a company releasing a model.
key_facts: Hearing held 13 October 2026 by the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, chaired by Liam Byrne
Anthropic (Liam Booth-Smith, head of Europe): 'The rules should be binding'
OpenAI (VP Tom Duff Gordon): relying only on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is not a good long-term plan; incident reporting should come first
Google DeepMind (Owen Larter) said to focus on standards; Meta (Rob Sherman) pointed to existing regulators
AISI director Henry de Zoete: AISI relies on cooperation and cannot block a release; Cabinet Office permanent secretary Cat Little confirmed the regime is voluntary
Byrne said the committee will look at an international convention, possibly pursued through the UK's coming G20 presidency
results.issues: The candidate named the committee 'Business and Trade'. Sources and Byrne himself call it the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) Committee. The parliament.uk page returned 403, so I could not check against the official record. The hearing details rest on Cyphrex and on search-result summaries of City AM, MLex and WIRED-based reports; Cyphrex was the only article I opened.

results.corrected_title: UK AI Security Institute regains pre-release access to frontier models after US reverses September block
results.corrected_summary: In September 2026 the White House told OpenAI, Anthropic and other labs to withhold new models from the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) until US officials had reviewed them, and Anthropic did not share Claude Mythos 5.1. The Daily Telegraph reported on 11 October that the US had reversed course after lobbying by UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan. On 12 October the UK government said AISI will keep testing the most powerful models before release. Narayan was cautious about whether the arrangement will last.
key_facts: September 2026: the White House asked labs to withhold new models from UK AISI pending US review
Anthropic did not give AISI full access to Claude Mythos 5.1 during the block
11 October: the Telegraph reported the reversal, crediting lobbying by AI minister Kanishka Narayan
12 October: the UK government confirmed AISI keeps pre-release access to frontier models
No formal US announcement was found; Narayan was cautious about whether it will last but 'very confident' the UK can test the latest models
results.issues: I did not open the original Telegraph report; the reversal is known from The Decoder and TNW, which also cites Bloomberg. The Decoder says access was restored for Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI. TNW mainly names OpenAI and Anthropic. At the 13 October hearing Anthropic said AISI now has access to Mythos 5.1, which supports the item. The block itself dates from September, so the news is the reversal reported 11-12 October. Overlaps with c037.

results.corrected_title: FTC sends civil investigative demands to OpenAI and Anthropic over AI safety incidents
results.corrected_summary: On Wednesday 14 October 2026, Axios reported, the US Federal Trade Commission sent civil investigative demands to OpenAI and Anthropic. They seek documents on AI safety incidents, safeguards, marketing materials and privacy policies, as part of a consumer-protection probe first reported around 30 September. An FTC spokesperson confirmed the subpoenas to CBS News, and OpenAI said it would 'engage constructively'. The demands do not mean either company broke the law.
key_facts: Demands sent on Wednesday 14 October 2026 (Axios report dated 15 October)
Each demand reportedly runs to more than 50 pages, covering security incidents, safeguarding practices, marketing and privacy policies
The FTC reportedly plans to compel top executives to testify and to send demands to third-party AI organisations
The probe was first reported by Axios on 30 September 2026; the demands are the new step
An FTC spokesperson confirmed the subpoenas to CBS News; OpenAI said 'We will engage constructively with the FTC'
results.issues: The Axios article dated 15 October returned 403, so I relied on TNW's reading of it, which cites a single unnamed source, plus TNW's account of the FTC confirmation to CBS. I did not open the CBS piece. The probe itself is from 30 September, before the window; only the 14 October demands are new. One outlet's claim that the FTC accused Anthropic of 'fraudulent' system usage is uncorroborated and left out. I did not check the TokenPost source or the claimed parallel EU action.
